items.title: RETHINKING PAKISTAN’S AUTO POLICY
items.description: For one woman interviewed for the 2019 social assessment of Karachi’s planned Yellow Line Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), getting to her job destination meant walking 20 minutes to a road crossing, paying for a rickshaw and then paying again for a bus. Other women interviewed for the assessment relied on shared three-wheelers that waited to fill up with passengers before leaving. For some, the journey could take two hours each way. Monthly transport costs ranged from Rs3,000 to Rs6,000 in households where incomes of Rs20,000 to Rs30,000 were common. Fares can eat into an already modest wage. An unreliable connection can make a worker late. A second fare at each end of the journey can make studying at a college or a job across town too expensive a proposition to take up. The draft for Pakistan’s Auto Policy 2026-31 revolves around car prices, manufacturers and tariffs. Yet, most households in the country own no car and struggle with the daily cost of commuting. Mobility for work, education and healthcare remains restricted due to unavailability of affordable and safe public transportation choices. How can Pakistan’s auto policy serve the people at large and not just the top decile of households in the country? THE FAULT IN OUR DRAFTS In April, when petrol rose by more than Rs137 a litre, governments briefly treated the price of a bus ticket as a cost-of-living issue. Islamabad announced 30 days of free public transport. Punjab’s relief ran for 69 days, with authorities estimating that hundreds of thousands of passengers a day used the free services. The relief ended, but the daily cost of getting to work remained. Pakistan now has a chance to address some of that cost through its next auto policy. The draft Auto Policy 2026-31 has been okayed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but is still awaiting final approval as the Ministry of Industries and Production is set to forward the draft policy to the Ministry of Finance, which aims to share it with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for review. This policy would reportedly reduce tariffs, open a formal route for commercial used-car imports and expand the role of electric vehicles. These changes could give car buyers more choice. The draft also shapes how buses and two-wheelers are taxed, which vehicles get incentives and where the proceeds of a proposed automobile levy go. The problem, in my view, is that the debate remains organised around the vehicle and its producer. The household experiences it as a sequence of fares, waits and transfers. An auto policy cannot run provincial bus services, but it can reduce fleet costs and make public support conditional on affordable service. That connects industrial policy to the ability to earn a living. Those decisions should be judged by what they do for the journeys people make every day. For most Pakistani households, the price of a bus ride is a more immediate concern than the price of a new car. WHO’S BUYING THE ALTO? Pakistan’s assemblers sold 155,631 passenger cars in 2025-26. Including separately reported jeeps and pick-ups takes four-wheeler sales to about 206,000. Motorcycle and rickshaw sales totalled roughly 1.97 million. My analysis of the 2024-25 Household Integrated Economic Survey (HIES) shows how differently Pakistanis get around. About 6.6 percent of households own a car and 57 percent own a motorcycle. Roughly 41 percent own neither. Among the poorest fifth of urban households, nearly two-thirds have neither vehicle and only about one in a thousand own a car. Among the richest urban fifth, more than one in five own a car. A Suzuki Alto VXR lists at about Rs2.99 million. The survey puts average household income at Rs82,179 a month, so the Alto costs more than three years of total income, before a household pays for food, rent or anything else. One reported estimate puts the likely reduction in small-car prices under the Auto Policy draft at around nine percent over five years. Applied to the Alto, that would still leave it costing about 33 months of average household income. There is a case for bringing those prices down faster. In 2006-07, local assemblers sold 180,834 cars, whereas passenger car sales reached just 155,631 in 2025-26. The figures are imperfectly comparable because classifications have changed and SUVs have become a bigger part of the market. Still, Indus Motors estimates that the industry can assemble about 600,000 vehicles a year and uses roughly 30 percent of that capacity. New manufacturers have entered the market, but factories still have far more capacity than the market can absorb. The entry of more assemblers does not by itself resolve this. If each operates a small plant behind similar tariff protection, the market can acquire more brands without acquiring the scale or price competition consumers need. Lower duties on finished cars would strengthen the pressure to compete, but duties on imported components also matter. A sensible transition should expose producers to competition while allowing them to obtain inputs at competitive prices. For some smaller imported cars, one reported tariff schedule keeps customs duty at 50 percent for the first two years and then brings it down in stages to 15 percent by 2030-31. Bringing those cuts forward would put earlier pressure on local producers to compete on price and quality. If the government also wants to discourage fuel-hungry vehicles, it can tax size or fuel use directly. A cut in customs duty does not translate directly into an equal cut in the showroom price. Exchange rates, other taxes and producer margins impact what the buyer pays. I would judge success by actual prices and product quality, rather than the number of assembly licences issued. A tariff timetable that can repeatedly be deferred offers consumers little assurance. Although Pakistan’s local car manufacturing capacity has more than doubled since 2006, annual sales (as denoted by the blue line) across the years have remained at a stagnated level | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the PIDE and the Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association (Pama) AN ELECTRIC SOLUTION? The distribution of electric vehicle incentives deserves the same scrutiny. Some reported proposals for electric cars include a favourable sales tax rate and a financing ceiling of Rs10 million. If a 17 percentage-point tax preference (the difference between tax rates on electric vehicles as compared to on an internal combustion engine vehicle) is applied to an Rs8 million pre-tax car, the buyer’s tax advantage would be Rs1.36 million. That is roughly the value of 21 electric-motorcycle subsidies of Rs65,000 each under the Pakistan Accelerated Vehicle Electrification (PAVE) programme. The actual benefit would depend on how the tax is applied and what the government ultimately approves. The comparison shows how much support can go to a single purchase. Equivalent fiscal support does not mean equal benefits from different vehicles. A higher loan ceiling does little for someone without a down payment or an income that a lender will accept. Eligibility matters as much as the advertised concession. Electric cars can cut petrol use, especially for people who drive long distances. But a household that cannot finance any private vehicle needs a different kind of help. A bus fare can determine whether someone in that household works at all. Car ownership remains heavily concentrated among wealthier households, while most urban Pakistanis in the lower income brackets have no personal vehicle | Author’s analysis of HIES 2024-25 data THE HIDDEN COST OF BEING UNABLE TO TRAVEL The poorest fifth of Pakistani households spent 4.8 percent of their budgets on transport, compared with 6.7 percent for the richest fifth. In cities, the respective figures are 4.2 and 6.5 percent. If spending were the measure of need, the figures would suggest transport was a bigger problem for the rich. But consider: a household survey counts the fare someone paid. It has no fare to record when a worker walks to save money, a woman turns down a job she cannot reach safely or a student stays home because college is too far away. The poorest fifth also spends almost half its budget on food, compared with about 29 percent for the richest fifth. Once food and the estimated rental value of housing are set aside, transport takes up a more similar share of what remains. The estimated rent includes the value of living in an owner-occupied home, even though no rent changes hands. Removing it from the comparison does not create cash for a bus ticket — it changes the denominator. I read the low transport share as a reason to investigate journeys people cannot make. The expenditure survey alone cannot tell us how many jobs were declined or classes missed. My analysis puts transport spending for the poorest fifth at about Rs254 per person a month. At Rs20 a ride, that pays for six complete return trips. A World Bank benchmark used in urban transport affordability studies allows for roughly 60 one-way trips a month. Even if someone in the poorest fifth put their entire transport budget towards a bus, they would still be well short of a month’s travel to work or school. Among poor urban households with at least one earner and neither a car nor a motorcycle, the survey implies about Rs9 in reported in-city fares per earner per working day. People may forget small fares when asked to recall spending over a year. The figures also cannot separate journeys made on foot from those abandoned altogether. Project documents for Karachi’s Red Line BRT estimate that about 40 percent of trips in the city are made on foot or by bicycle. Some people choose to walk or cycle. For others, it may be the only way to avoid paying for several rides on a single journey. The cost is easier to see against a wage. My analysis of the survey puts median monthly earnings for an urban paid worker at about Rs32,000. At Rs80 each way over 26 working days, the commute costs Rs4,160, or 13 percent of pay. A combination of wagons and rickshaws costing Rs200 a day takes Rs5,200, or more than 16 percent of pay. At the household level, two earners, each paying Rs20 in both directions over 26 working days, would spend Rs2,080 a month. Against the roughly Rs40,146 monthly budget for the poorest urban households in my analysis, that is just over five percent. At Rs80, the same journeys cost Rs8,320, or about 21 percent. These comparisons use survey-period budgets and illustrative fares, not today’s measured burden. They show why a fare that looks modest per trip can be unaffordable when paid repeatedly. For women in paid urban work, reported median monthly earnings were about Rs10,000, partly reflecting fewer hours of paid work. A 26-day commute at Rs80 each way would take about 42 percent of that amount. This is an illustration, since a woman earning Rs10,000 may work fewer days. It shows what fares can do to the gains from taking on more work. Distance can also put education out of reach. In the survey, about 1.3 million girls and young women and 900,000 boys and young men aged five to 24 had never attended school and cited distance as the reason. Where there is a school to go to, a safe, affordable journey can remove one of the barriers to getting there. Motorcycle ownership only partly solves this problem. A single motorcycle cannot necessarily serve two earners travelling in different directions and children going to school. Nor can we assume that every household member can ride it. Therefore, counting households with a vehicle tells us less than knowing who can use it, when and for which journeys. The economics of commuting favours public transport, as demonstrated by this comparison across one month | Author’s analysis of data sourced from the World Bank, PIDE and HIES A BUS PEOPLE CAN RELY ON On Lahore’s Orange Line train, about 51 percent of reported journeys were for work and 33 percent for education. In Peshawar, a 2023 account citing TransPeshawar (a public company established by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to manage, operate and maintain the Zu Peshawar BRT system) put women at about 30 percent of passengers on the bus rapid transit system, up from an estimated two percent on earlier services. Other published accounts put the newer figure closer to 20 percent. The new system offered separate entrances and reserved areas, better lighting, station security and more predictable service. Research in Lahore by economists Robert Garlick, Erica Field and Kate Vyborny offers a closer look at how transport impacts decisions about work. Through a job-search platform, the researchers offered commuting services to women. The offer of women-only transport more than doubled job application rates, while mixed-gender transport produced little response. The study measured applications, not jobs secured. It shows how the commute can deter women before an employer has even seen their names. Even a new bus can be difficult to board. Writing in Eos earlier this year, Samina Hassan Laghari and Arif Hasan described Karachi’s electric buses with about 30 seats carrying 70 or 80 people, sometimes more than 100. Women told them they had given up work because of the journey. The city’s bus fleet was reported at 1,029, against an estimated requirement of 15,000. Building more corridors can help, but people have to reach them. A cheap fare on the main route can lose much of its value if a passenger has to pay for a rickshaw to get to it. A well-lit stop is of limited use to a child who has to cross a dangerous road to reach it. The World Health Organisation (WHO) estimates roughly 28,000 road deaths a year in Pakistan, with pedestrians accounting for a large share. Official reported totals are much lower. Both the walk to the bus and the ride itself belong in a transport plan. Reliability matters as much as the fare. A daily-wage worker who cannot tell whether a bus will arrive in five minutes or 45 has to leave early or risk losing a shift. Karachi’s Red Line has faced a much longer timetable than originally envisaged. While cities build major corridors, they also need buses running between neighbourhoods, regular departures and connections that people can use without building an hour’s uncertainty into the day. A dependable service also reduces the unpaid time a worker must allow for delays. Time savings belong in the economic appraisal, even when they produce no additional fare revenue. They should be measured through actual waiting and journey times, rather than assumed whenever a new bus or corridor is announced. THE COST OF THE COMMUTE To compare the choices, I modelled the same trip across five modes, with 30 kilometres covered a day, 26 days a month. For private vehicles, the calculation includes ownership and financing costs as well as fuel or electricity. For the bus passenger, it includes a low main fare and some travel to and from the route. Under these assumptions, monthly costs per commuter are roughly Rs1,900 for a bus, Rs4,900 for an electric motorcycle, Rs5,200 for wagons and rickshaws, Rs7,000 for a petrol motorcycle and Rs39,900 for a small petrol car. The bus estimate includes a Rs25 fare and feeder journeys. The model assumes petrol at Rs378 a litre, 15 percent vehicle financing and some sharing of private vehicles. These are modelled costs, not quoted monthly instalments. The bus figure is what the passenger pays after public support; it is not the full cost of providing the service. The difference matters for the country’s import bill as well as the commuter’s wallet. Pakistan spent about $16.9 billion on petroleum imports in fiscal year (FY)26, compared with roughly $2.1 billion on imported vehicle assembly kits. The totals cover different categories, but they give a sense of the scale of dependence on imported fuel. In the model, moving one million daily commuters from motorcycles into small petrol cars would add about Rs394 billion a year to household costs and roughly $440 million to imports, including fuel and vehicles. Electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes. In the model, each rupee of public support for electric motorcycles saves households more cash and generally saves more on imports than a rupee spent on buses. A bus reaches people a motorcycle subsidy cannot readily serve, including students, older passengers and households that cannot buy a vehicle. That makes a case for supporting both. The journey being replaced matters. A bus carrying former wagon passengers has a different effect on imports from one attracting motorists. An electric motorcycle replacing a petrol motorcycle is different from an additional vehicle bought for convenience. My calculations assume those substitutions — they are not a forecast that every subsidised purchase will deliver the same saving. I would assess the programmes against what riders actually stop using. There is a case for electric buses on routes where charging and electricity supply can support them. In an illustrative comparison, a diesel bus covering 80,000 kilometres a year uses about 18,000 litres of fuel. At the diesel price of Rs395.20 a litre, effective on November 3, that costs about Rs7.1 million. Meanwhile, an electric bus, using about 96,000 units of power at an assumed Rs39.70 per unit, would spend about Rs3.8 million on electricity. The roughly Rs3.3 million difference comes before maintenance, financing and battery costs. A city weighing the higher purchase price should count that annual saving and the reduced exposure to a diesel price spike. Battery replacements and charging equipment also belong in the calculation. High utilisation helps recover the higher purchase price only if charging arrangements allow buses to run the promised service. Electric buses eliminate exhaust at the roadside, but overall emissions also depend on electricity generation. A national pollution claim needs a separate estimate. Women and men pictured driving electric bikes in Lahore: electric motorcycles offer substantial savings where people already ride petrol bikes | White Star HOW MANY BUSES CAN A LEVY BUY? The Automotive Development Levy (ADL), proposed in the draft for the Auto Policy 2026-31, could raise around Rs232 billion over five years. Its reported uses include export rebates and industrial upgrading. The government should consider putting a share towards public transport and say which proposed uses it would scale back to do so. Spread evenly, the projected revenue comes to about Rs46 billion a year. In my model, an electric bus running around 70,000 kilometres a year with 800 passenger boardings a day needs about Rs21.5 million in annual public support if borrowing costs 18 percent. At 11 percent, the contribution falls by about Rs5.5 million, to roughly Rs16 million. At that lower cost, the entire annual levy could support close to 2,900 buses. Using only a share would pay for proportionately fewer. The levy still needs approval and the figures depend on what buses cost, how much operators collect in fares and how many people ride. The assumptions also deserve scrutiny before anyone commits public money. Eight hundred boardings are not 800 different people: a commuter travelling both ways boards twice. At Rs25 a ride and 312 operating days, 800 daily boardings produce Rs6.24 million in annual fare revenue. If boardings halve, that revenue falls by Rs3.12 million, while much of the cost of owning the fleet remains. The model also assumes non-fare revenue at 37 percent of fares, which requires testing against actual advertising receipts. The 11 percent financing rate is an assumption rather than a financing commitment. Any interest subsidy must be funded and a guarantee can leave the state liable if repayments fail. Supporting 15,000 buses on those terms would cost around Rs240 billion a year. That is a recurring public expense. Pakistani households already spend an estimated Rs2.37 trillion a year on transport, according to the household survey. The question for the government is how much of that spending on a better service could save households and which trips people could make if the fare came down or the bus turned up regularly. Household savings cannot simply be netted against the government’s subsidy bill. A lower fare partly shifts costs from passengers to taxpayers — it does not eliminate them. Nor is all of the Rs2.37 trillion available to finance urban buses. The economic case must rest on savings in fuel and time, safer journeys and better access to work, alongside a credible plan for meeting the recurring budget commitment. WHAT THE POLICY NEEDS The policy can start by reconsidering the reported two percent development levy on buses and reviewing duties on electric buses and charging equipment. It can give affordable electric motorcycles and rickshaws greater priority in vehicle incentives. And it can make bus funding conditional on the service that provincial authorities and operators deliver. Localisation targets also need care. A rule designed around a petrol engine can penalise an electric motorcycle because its battery is imported. I would reward the value actually created in Pakistan, with a transition that allows battery and component suppliers to develop. The aim should be competitive suppliers that can sell beyond one protected domestic market. For bus funding, that means setting routes, fares and safety standards, then paying operators for running the scheduled service and maintaining the fleet. Provinces would have to pay on time and operators would have to run the promised service. Passengers should be able to see how often buses ran, how long they waited, and how many services were cancelled. Cities should also track who uses the system and ask people which journeys they still cannot make. A contract can make those obligations enforceable. The province could retain fare revenue and pay an operator for service delivered, with deductions for missed trips and safety failures. That reduces the incentive to overcrowd buses but leaves the province carrying the risk of weak ridership. Payment reserves and dependable budget releases would be necessary — private finance does not remove that obligation. Depots and power connections must be ready when the fleet arrives. I would begin with routes where demand can be tested, publish the results and expand where the service earns continued support. I would also want a travel survey to test the arguments made here. If low reported spending chiefly reflects short, affordable journeys and incomplete recall, the case for suppressed travel (when individuals do not undertake trips or activities due to barriers or constraints) would weaken. If well-run buses attract few riders, routes and spending should be reconsidered. A policy should allow those findings to change where the next rupee goes. Pakistan can keep a tally of cars coming off assembly lines. Over the next five years, it should also count how many more people can get to a job, a classroom or a clinic without buying a vehicle. For a woman making that journey, it comes down to what happens after the 20-minute walk: how long she waits, whether there’s room to get on and how much of her pay she has left when she gets home. The writer is a macroeconomist and professor of practice at IBA, Karachi. He can be reached at ammar.habib@gmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, November 8th, 2026

items.title: Siblings acquitted in blasphemy case after 20 years
items.description: • SC sets aside death sentences upheld by LHC • Observes findings on mental illness raise doubts about culpability ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Saturday acquitted two brothers in a blasphemy case under Section 295-C of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), setting aside their death sentences earlier upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) over a decade ago. A three-judge SC bench, headed by Chief Justice of Pakistan Yahya Afridi and comprising Justices Shakeel Ahmad and Ishtiaq Ibrahim, took up criminal appeals against the Sept 17, 2015 decision of the LHC. The brothers, Liaqat Ali and Umar Draz, have spent around 20 years behind bars. They were convicted by a sessions judge in Jhang on March 27, 2006. The trial court sentenced both brothers to death and imposed a fine of Rs500,000 each, with five years’ rigorous imprisonment in default. The high court dismissed their appeals and upheld the convictions. The main SC judgement was authored by Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim. Justice Shakeel Ahmad concurred with the order but also annexed an additional note. According to the complaint, Umar Draz had begun making explicit blasphemous statements, leading to a marital dispute between him and his wife that culminated in divorce on March 13, 2006. Draz explicitly affirmed in writing his conversion from Islam in the divorce papers. During the return of his former wife’s dowry articles, a written document auth­ored by co-appellant Liaqat Ali was recovered. It also contained blasphemous assertions. On March 18, 2006, when the complainant and witnesses confronted the brothers over the alleged blasphemous material, both appellants acknowledged and verified the contents of the documents and unequivocally declared their willingness to reiterate their assertions before any forum. Before the SC, their counsel confined his submissions to the plea of mental unsoundness, arguing that the appellants lacked the requisite mens rea (guilty mind) at the time of the alleged offence. The SC examined three psychiatric assessments. An initial three-member medical board at DHQ Hospital, Faisalabad, found both appellants mentally sound in 2007. However, an eight-member Board of Certification diagnosed them with “bipolar affective disorder with psychotic symptoms” in 2023. A nine-member Board of Certification in September 2025 concluded that both brothers were suffering from “bipolar disorder current episode manic”. It described the condition as a chronic illness that was most likely permanent in acute cases, with absent insight and an inability to understand their acts at the time. The SC observed that the unanimous opinions of specialised boards comprising senior professors of psychiatry carried greater weight than the earlier assessm­ent by a board with only one psychiatrist. It also noted that bipolar disorder was episodic and had a genetic component, and that both brothers had been independently diagnosed with the same condition. “The appellants have spent around 20 years behind bars. In the light of the opinion of medical board which raises doubts regarding the culpability of the appellants, the benefit of doubt cannot be withheld from the appellants,” the judgement said. While acquitting the appellants, the SC also expected the executive director of the Punjab Institute of Mental Health, Lahore, to ensure that their medical treatment was not discontinued. Additional note In his concurring note, Justice Ahmad agreed with the acquittal but cautioned that a psychiatric diagnosis alone did not satisfy the requirements of Section 84 of the PPC. The judge distinguished medical insanity from legal insanity, noting that the key question was whether, at the time of the offence, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. He argued that legal accountability had to be balanced with humanity, explaining that true justice also included mercy when the law recognised a person’s lack of mental capacity. The note said the medical reports, along with the surrounding circumstances, created reasonable doubt. It also referred to Islamic principles of legal capacity and responsibility. Published in Dawn, November 8th, 2026

items.title: Un réseau de blanchiment tombe en Algérie : 50 millions DA, des devises et des armes saisis
items.description: L’Algérie poursuit sa guerre totale contre les réseaux de blanchiment d’argent . Les opérations spectaculaires se multiplient. La dernière en date a été menée samedi par les services de sécurité de l’Armée nationale populaire en 5ᵉ Région militaire (Constantine). Elle s’est soldée par le démantèlement d’un réseau criminel organisé spécialisé dans le blanchiment d’argent, la saisie d’importantes sommes d’argent en dinars et en euros, d’armes à feu ainsi que l’arrestation de 8 suspects. Blanchiment d’argent en Algérie : un réseau tombe dans l’Est du pays « Cette opération s’est soldée par l’arrestation de huit personnes et la saisie de sommes d’argent en monnaie nationale s’élevant à près de cinq milliards de centimes (50 millions de DA), ainsi que 45.125 euros et diverses sommes en devises étrangères. Aussi, il a été procédé à la saisie d’une quantité d’or estimée à 1,861 kilogramme, de huit véhicules touristiques et de quatre fusils de chasse, en sus d’autres effets utilisés dans des opérations de blanchiment d’argent », a indiqué le ministère de la Défense nationale dans un communiqué. Cette opération de « qualité confirme, une fois de plus, la mobilisation de l’ensemble des unités de l’Armée nationale populaire, afin de contrecarrer toutes les tentatives visant à porter atteinte à l’économie nationale », a ajouté la même source. L’Algérie a considérablement durci sa réglementation de lutte contre le blanchiment d’argent. En parallèle, les services de sécurité ont multiplié les opérations spectaculaires contre les réseaux de blanchiment et ont récupéré d’importantes sommes d’argent. L’article Un réseau de blanchiment tombe en Algérie : 50 millions DA, des devises et des armes saisis est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Employ us or face Jubilee House protest in two weeks – Graduates with disabilities
items.description: The Coalition of Unemployed Graduates with Disabilities has given the government two weeks to employ its qualified members in the public sector or secure financial clearance for their recruitment in the upcoming national budget. The group has warned that failure to meet either demand will trigger a three-day continuous demonstration at Jubilee House. In a press statement signed by its Group Convener, Gilbert Boateng Agyare, the coalition accused the government of failing to honour commitments made over the past eight months following a series of engagements on the employment of its members. The coalition said its latest ultimatum followed unsuccessful attempts to secure concrete action, despite assurances from government representatives that qualified graduates with disabilities would be absorbed into the public workforce. According to the group, the government first made a commitment to facilitate their employment after members staged a demonstration in March 2026. It said it subsequently suspended the protest in good faith, but the promised recruitment did not materialise. The coalition explained that it later organised a second demonstration to demand action, after which government representatives requested a comprehensive list of qualified graduates for consideration. It said it submitted the list and was subsequently informed that it had been forwarded to the President. However, the group expressed disappointment that no concrete progress had been communicated weeks after the submission. “Every single pledge made to this coalition over the past eight months has proven to be totally futile,” the statement said. The coalition accused government representatives of engaging protesters mainly to bring demonstrations to an end, without following through on the commitments made. “ We are declaring today that our patience is completely exhausted. We will no longer tolerate being used for photo opportunities or pacified by meaningless political rhetoric while qualified citizens with disabilities languish in enforced poverty and unemployment,” the statement added. Two-week ultimatum The coalition is demanding that the government complete the recruitment and placement of all qualified graduates on its submitted list into public sector institutions within two weeks. Alternatively, it wants the government to secure financial clearance for their employment in the forthcoming national budget. The group warned that failure to meet either demand within the stipulated period would lead to a three-day uninterrupted demonstration at Jubilee House. It said protesters would remain at the seat of government until every graduate on the submitted list received a verifiable employment letter. “We will not vacate the seat of government, nor will we be pacified by emergency meetings or verbal pledges. We will remain at the gates of Jubilee House until every single graduate on our list receives verifiable employment letters,” the statement warned. Graduates reject charity, demand equal opportunities The coalition said its members had overcome significant challenges to obtain university degrees and diplomas, including inaccessible infrastructure and non-inclusive educational environments. It said their academic achievements and professional qualifications should give them an opportunity to contribute to national development and earn a decent living. “We did not let our physical constraints stop us from pursuing higher education. We climbed staircases without ramps, sat through non-inclusive lecture halls, navigated unsupportive environments, and defied every societal expectation to earn our university degrees and diplomas,” the statement said. The group stressed that its members were not seeking charity but equal opportunities to work, support their families and live independently. “We do not want sympathy or charity. We demand opportunity, fairness, and justice,” it added. Coalition appeals to traditional and religious leaders The group has appealed to traditional authorities, religious leaders, civil society organisations and human rights advocates to intervene and help resolve the matter. Among those it called upon were the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II; the Okyenhene, Osagyefo Amoatia Ofori Panin; and the Dormaahene, Oseadeeyo Agyeman Badu II, as well as the leadership of the National House of Chiefs. It also appealed to the National Chief Imam, Sheikh Osman Nuhu Sharubutu; the Christian Council of Ghana; the Ghana Catholic Bishops’ Conference; and the National Peace Council to use their influence to advocate for the rights of graduates with disabilities. The coalition further called on former Vice-President Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, the Council of State, civil society organisations and governance watchdogs to support its campaign, insisting that the issue should transcend political affiliations. It maintained that the employment of persons with disabilities was a human rights and social justice issue requiring urgent national attention. The statement ended with a renewed appeal to the President to direct the release and posting of the graduates on the submitted list, warning that the coalition would proceed with its planned demonstration if the government failed to act within two weeks. “Enough of the empty talk. Act now, or prepare to meet us at Jubilee House,” Mr Agyare said on behalf of the coalition.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : quatre lutteurs sénégalais à l’assaut de nouvelles médailles
items.description: Après une journée faste, ponctuée par deux nouvelles médailles d’or, le Sénégal entend poursuivre sa moisson aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Quatre jeunes athlètes sont attendus, ce dimanche 8 novembre, sur les tapis de lutte de plage, avec l’ambition d’enrichir le tableau des médailles du pays hôte. La dynamique est lancée et les jeunes Sénégalais comptent bien la maintenir. Après les performances remarquables enregistrées en lutte de plage, avec les sacres d’Élisabeth Diatta et de Maguette Diop, le Sénégal retourne à l’arène ce dimanche pour une nouvelle journée de compétition. Quatre représentants nationaux sont en lice pour tenter de décrocher de nouvelles médailles devant leur public. Chez les filles, Ndeye Khady Anna Diatta, 17 ans, défendra les couleurs nationales dans la catégorie des moins de 45 kg. Sa compatriote Mery Manga, également âgée de 17 ans, sera engagée chez les moins de 65 kg. Du côté masculin, Ibrahima Sarr, 16 ans, tentera de s'illustrer dans la catégorie des moins de 70 kg. Ablaye Diouf, 17 ans, complétera la délégation sénégalaise chez les moins de 90 kg.Après les premiers exploits de leurs compatriotes, ces quatre jeunes lutteurs ont désormais l'occasion de prolonger l'élan et de faire vibrer davantage le public sénégalais. items.title: Ghana’s WEAR Ghana and Republic of Africa emerge winners at CANEX Creative Pitch 2026
items.description: Ghanaian creative entrepreneur Awura Abena Agyeman has emerged victorious at the CANEX Creative Pitch 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, following a presentation on the journey of WEAR Ghana and its evolution into the pan-African cultural enterprise, Republic of Africa. The competition formed part of Creative Africa Nexus Weekend (CANEX WKND), organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank). The gathering brings together entrepreneurs, artists, investors, policymakers and other stakeholders to explore opportunities for financing, collaboration and growth across Africa’s creative industries. Awura Abena Agyeman’s presentation traced the evolution of WEAR Ghana, established in 2013 to encourage greater appreciation for locally produced clothing, into a business that has combined contemporary fashion with African cultural identity. Among its notable successes is the GIGI, a collection incorporating African wax-print details, which became a signature product following its introduction in 2016 and is still selling around the world, 10 years later. The presentation also introduced the broader vision behind Republic of Africa, launched in May 2025 as a pan-African cultural initiative seeking to connect people across borders through fashion, creativity and shared identity. Beyond the business journey, Awura Abena Agyeman highlighted the importance of employment, skills development and local production in creating opportunities within Africa’s creative economy. Her recognition at CANEX comes amid growing conversations about the economic potential of African creativity and the need for stronger local participation in the industries built around the continent’s cultural influence. The achievement also underscores the role of platforms such as CANEX in creating opportunities for African creative entrepreneurs to engage directly with potential investors and industry leaders. For WEAR Ghana and the Republic of Africa, the victory represents another chapter in a journey that began with a simple ambition to encourage Ghanaians to wear Ghanaian-made clothing and has since grown into a wider vision of African cultural connection and enterprise.

items.title: BEDC announces salary increase for staff
items.description: Benin Electricity Distribution Company (BEDC) Plc has announced salary increases for all staff following an agreement with two recognised labour unions, effective Dec. 1. This is contained in a statement issued by the management of the electricity distribution firm on Sunday in Benin. The agreement was reached at a meeting between the company’s management, the National Union of Electricity Employees (NUEE) and the Senior Staff Association of Electricity and Allied Companies (SSAEAC) on Nov. 6. The meeting was led by BEDC’s Acting Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Mr Jonathan Lawani. SSAEAC was represented by its Deputy General Secretary, Comrade Innocent Lord-Douglas, while NUEE was represented by Comrade Mbang Ntukubes. Lawani, in the statement, said the successful conclusion of negotiations, which began in March, demonstrated management’s commitment to staff welfare and improved organisational performance. “The successful conclusion of this joint negotiation and review process reflects our shared commitment to staff welfare and the overall performance of BEDC,” he said. He, however, described the recent industrial action by workers as avoidable, saying it resulted in revenue losses, reputational damage and hardship for electricity consumers. Lawani expressed regret that the industrial action occurred before the agreed date for concluding negotiations, as reaffirmed at the Oct. 7 meeting. He also explained that BEDC’s approved operational expenditure framework had remained fundamentally unchanged since 2013, in spite of rising costs and prevailing economic realities. According to him, access to the company’s full approved operational expenditure allocation depends on meeting prescribed collection performance thresholds, while shortfalls result in reduced allocations. The management said the explanation underscored the company’s financial constraints and the need to balance employees’ welfare with business sustainability. BEDC commended the leadership of NUEE and SSAEAC for their cooperation and constructive engagement in reaching an amicable resolution. The company reaffirmed its commitment to transparency, mutual respect and industrial harmony, describing employee welfare as central to its transformation agenda. It said the agreement represented a step towards strengthening trust, collaboration and shared responsibility between management and organised labour The post BEDC announces salary increase for staff appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La machine du nectar d’arts ( 2/2)
items.description: « Je suis le moins créatif de cette équipe, le moins intéressant. Je travaillais avec des gens dont je suis fan. Ce n’est pas l’œuvre de Xalil, mais d’une équipe. J’étais juste derrière pour arbitrer. À la fin, on s’est retrouvé avec cette œuvre collective qui nous ressemble et nous rassemble », introduit Xalil quand on lui demande de présenter son équipe, dont personne n’avait jusqu’ici jamais organisé ou assisté à des cérémonies de Jeux olympiques. Lire aussi: Le « Nandité » aux commandes d’une académie (1/2) D’abord le metteur en scène, Adama Diop. « Il est à lui seul une machine, ce mec », s’exclame Xalil, qui ne connaissait pas cet acteur du théâtre avant de le contacter. « J’ai fait mes recherches et suis tombé sur lui. Je ne cherchais pas forcément quelqu’un de fou, mais d’un génie qui en voulait et qui était prêt à s’engager. Et quand j’ai vu qu’il a implanté une école et entendu son discours de lancement, je me suis que c’est lui qu’il me faut. Il n’habite pas toute l’année Dakar, mais il était super chaud quand je l’ai appelé pour représenter l’Afrique », confie Xalil Cissé, à qui Adama Diop a proposé de travailler sur la symbolique du cercle. Le cercle qui renvoie au bol en Afrique, à la cour du roi, aux assemblées…, mais rejoignent aussi les cinq anneaux olympiques. Ensuite, il y a Marième Ngom, coordinatrice générale Hmc (habillage, maquillage, coiffure), qui jouit d’une solide expérience dans l’écosystème du cinéma et de la mode. Selon Xalil, c’était un vrai soulagement d’avoir une personne qui comprenait rapidement et savait où elle allait avant même d’emprunter le chemin. D’ailleurs, Xalil précise que, hormis Adama Diop qu’il ne connaissait pas, il connaissait tout le reste de l’équipe qui était des noms qui s’imposaient à lui au fil de l’écriture du projet. La certitude s’est encore mieux affirmée avec les designers qui ont géré les trois temps de la cérémonie. Maguette Gueye de la Penderie de Maam, Khadija Bâ de L’Artisane et Selly Raby Kane. « Pour ces trois femmes, je n’ai même pas cherché à négocier. Il me les fallait absolument dans l’équipe », sourit Xalil Cissé. Maguette Gueye a habillé le Temps 1 de la cérémonie avec La Penderie de Maam, concernant tout ce qui touche au patrimoine, le sens de grandir sur l’Afrique. Elle a réalisé tous les costumes de cet acte, que ce soient les lutteurs, le tambour-major, les danseurs, AlKebulan, etc. Pour le Temps 2, qui raconte aujourd’hui, Khadija Bâ L’Artisane s’en est occupée. Elle est porteuse d’un style particulier, très réfléchi, qui valse entre modernité et patrimoine. Elle est surtout un as du fait-main, et son œuvre donne à résolument visualiser l’image urbaine dans son évolution spatio-temporelle. Selly Raby Kane, qui a vêtu le Temps 3, est déjà notoire dans le monde. Pour sa folie créatrice, son approche futuriste, son génie à poser des éléments du décor qui n’existent encore pas. Une constellation de lumières Quand Xalil Cissé parle d’Ismaïla Talla alias Iss 814, le directeur musical, on sent encore les étoiles dans les yeux. Il est clairement fasciné. « Ce mec, je l’appelle juste pour lui dire que j’ai besoin d’un directeur musical dans le projet artistique. Aussitôt je termine mon propos, comme un vrai génie, Iss 814 me fait un nombre incalculable de propositions, me dit comment le son doit être travaillé, comment doit se soutenir le rythme, etc. Il est même allé, dans ce même entretien téléphonique, à dessiner une trame de la cérémonie. Je me suis dit que je tiens mon gars moi », dit Xalil dans un éclat de rire qui signifie amusement et admiration. Iss 814, d’après lui, estimait qu’il lui manquait que cette corde à accomplir et accordait plus d’attention à ce moment que les disques d’or qu’il a déjà gagnés. Cette estime réciproque n’a pas cependant empêché qu’ils se sont chamaillés le long du projet, car « Iss 814 est tellement talentueux et fou qu’il court plus que la vitesse requise ». Eux deux laissaient libre cours à leur folie au studio. « On s’amusait un peu. On se disait par exemple essayons Saalimtoo, et bim ! il réécrit le thème et compose un truc de dingue », se souvient Xalil. Ainsi ont-ils eu leur musique de toute la première partie. Ensuite, puisqu’il fallait assumer la musique sous la férule du patrimoine africain, ils sont allés chercher des artistes et pris de vrais instruments pour rejouer toute la musique composée par Iss 814. Ouais, il fallait que le sabar, le tama, et tutti quanti disent leurs droits. Ensuite, il y a Khady Kassé, la scénographe. C’est elle qui a réalisé tous les éléments de scénographie physique sur cette performance. Elle est arrivée un peu tard dans le projet, mais a su s’y coller parfaitement selon le directeur artistique. Khady Kassé a été la scénographe de la 15e édition de la Biennale de l’art africain contemporain de Dakar, qui entame sa 16e édition dans moins de deux semaines (19 novembre – 19 décembre). Xalil Cissé avait l’atout d’avoir travaillé sur l’ouverture du Stade Abdoulaye Wade. Il connaissait donc l’endroit et avait identifié son espace. Les équipes techniques, qui capitalisaient plein d’événements dans ce stade, avaient également une parfaite maîtrise de ses infrastructures, « ce qui permettait une avance considérable malgré les délais relativement courts qui nous étaient impartis ». Il y avait par ailleurs une déambulation à la fin, qui était tel un défilé de modes. C’était quelque peu l’idée, une idée réalisée par neuf stylistes. Ils ont pour noms Rashid, Donatela Crea, Niuku, Stef de Karda, Weuz Owens, Gelisa Georges, Radji Radji, Jeyna A et Carmena A. « Ce sont de jeunes créateurs qui sont venus prêter main-forte avec 50 tenues, pour la fin très impactante de ce temps, suivant la direction artistique », explique Xalil Cissé. Dakar dans le «Dakar 2026» L’idée de Dakar, dans son authentique actualité urbaine, est transparue dans la performance. D’abord, la figure d’Issa Ramangellisa Samb Joe Ouakam, incarnée par l’artiste Obree Daman (Omar Samb de son vrai nom, par ailleurs parent de Joe Ouakam). « Il était très heureux d’avoir ce rôle, parce qu’il est aussi de la famille de Joe Ouakam. Puis il l’a très bien portée. Vous avez vu la pipe, la tenue ? », s’extasie encore Xalil, qui raconte qu’Obree Daman s’est aussitôt mis dans l’idée du designer. Et que dire des scènes de vie de Dakar ? Au-delà du clin à « Madame Brouette » de Moussa Sène Absa, c’est tous ces « pousse-pousse » (chariots à café) qui font le décor de la capitale, les « forox caaya », le tohu-bohu urbain, l’encombrement du piéton, les commerces sauvages, les petits larcins et le « tek xel », etc. « Tout cela c’est la ville, c’est Dakar », dit Xalil Cissé. Après la cérémonie, au milieu des satisfactions, beaucoup de spectateurs ont relevé la « cacophonie de la fin », considérant que l’équipe artistique s’est relâchée au terme du spectacle. En vérité, cette scène est un vrai faux capharnaüm, selon le directeur artistique. « Vous voyez, tout était ordonné, maîtrisé et réglé comme sur du papier à musique. On voulait montrer qu’on peut très bien, que tous les Africains peuvent très bien faire. Mais nous péchons souvent dans la finition. Nous avons un problème pour bien terminer. C’est cette image que nous voulions poser. Dire aux gens voilà, nous avons parlé au monde, maintenant parlons franchement entre nous. Voilà notre propre turpitude. N’est-ce pas notre sentiment quand nous circulons dans Dakar ? », questionne Xalil Cissé. L’art du désordre dans l’ordre. La claque sur les Sénégalais. Pour leur dire que « Voilà vous » ! « L’art, c’est aussi peindre une société. Relever des trucs qui ne sont pas bien », répète Xalil. N’est-ce pas aussi là que l’entrée du jeune artiste VJ tonne toute sa pertinence. Lui qui, entre le désordre médiatique et politique, a frayé un chemin où l’a retrouvé toute une jeune génération sans crier gare. Voilà, l’image d’une jeunesse qui émerge, même dans l’incertitude et le chaos. Un cosmogramme qui fait sens et plaisir La cérémonie d’ouverture des Joj « Dakar 2026 » était grandiose. Ce, par la fluidité d’une réalisation ayant rassemblé plus d’un millier de talents. 25 artistes et solistes, 54 performers, 32 acteurs et comédiens, 628 danseurs, 373 figurants, deux maîtres de cérémonie (Oumy Ndour pour la partie francophone et Y Dee pour l’anglophone), avec un plateau presque paritaire (45% de femmes pour 55% d’hommes). Puis, il y a eu les artistes vedettes. « Le choix de Kiné Lam, parce que je pense qu’il n’y a personne pour porter cette voix mieux que cette dame. On pourrait en dire autant pour Baaba Maal, qui est une voix panafricaine », pense Xalil Cissé. Le choix des artistes s’est fait depuis l’écriture du projet. Le directeur artistique privilégiait les artistes avec une écriture visuelle, dont l’expression artistique fait défiler dans l’esprit du spectateur des images s’adressant directement à sa sensibilité. C’est un narratif pour le continent. Et il fallait des artistes qui incarnent cette idée de l’Afrique. L’entrée d’Obree Daman, Maah Keïta (bass) et Sona Jobarteh (kora) était une transition entre deux temps. Il fallait des artistes modernes, porteurs de symboles puissants pour offrir un spectacle qui ne devait juste ne pas être pour les oreilles. L’inclusion était un maître-mot. L’Afrique qui rejoint l’universel était un impératif. Sona Jobarteh était donc là, musicienne dont la kora conquiert les scènes du monde. Souleymane Faye, quoique considéré comme marginal, reste un artiste avec une voix collective et attachante à notre imaginaire. Que dire de Kya Loum, dont la déclamation de l’hymne national a même fait frémir les moins patriotes ? La lutte sénégalaise, le « lamb », a aussi été un marqueur majuscule. Ce sport de chez a exposé sa panoplie culturelle, au travers du « bàkk », geste chorégraphique d’auto-détermination qui permet au guerrier ou au lutteur de dire sa puissance et lancer vaillamment un défi. À côté, il y a eu la prestation du « simb », le « faux-lion », notre cirque local qui saisit l’imaginaire de tout urbain. Par Mamadou Oumar KAMARA

items.title: Attentat à Cracovie : six morts, trois corps trouvés au domicile du tireur et des étrangers parmi les victimes
items.description: Le 7 novembre, vers 15h, heure locale, un attentat terroriste s'est produit pres de la place principale de Cracovie, ville du sud de la Pologne. Un homme a ouvert le feu sur des passants au hasard depuis une voiture. Selon les dernieres informations, six personnes ont trouve la mort, parmi lesquelles, d'apres le ministere polonais des Affaires etrangeres, un ressortissant britannique ainsi que deux femmes de nationalite polonaise. Au moins 15 autres personnes ont ete blessees, dont 12 se trouvent dans un etat grave. L'ambassade de Russie en Pologne a indique qu'une citoyenne russe figurait parmi les blesses. Il y a egalement des policiers parmi les victimes, dont l'un se trouve dans un etat grave. Un Polonais d'extreme droite âge de 24 ans, qui a tue sa famille avant l'attentat Selon le ministre polonais de l'Interieur, Marcin Kerviński, le tireur etait un citoyen polonais de 24 ans, adepte de l'ideologie d'extreme droite. Il etait vetu d'un treillis, d'un gilet pare-balles et d'un casque. L'homme a tire avec une arme a canon long, vraisemblablement un fusil semi-automatique AR-15. Selon la porte-parole de la police de Cracovie, Katarzyna Cislo, le tireur disposait egalement d'une arme de rechange et d'une grande quantite de munitions. L'agresseur a ete blesse lors de son arrestation et hospitalise. Vídeo completo de la neutralización del atacante en Cracovia. #krakow #poland https://t.co/Cjhzu6rXL9 — RO-1 (@Undercover_Camo) November 7, 2026 Plus tard, la police polonaise a decouvert trois autres corps dans l'appartement du tireur : un homme de 53 ans et deux femmes âgees respectivement de 52 et 21 ans. Une fois leur identite etablie, il s'est avere que les victimes etaient le pere, la mere et la sœur de l'agresseur. Le Premier ministre polonais, Donald Tusk, a qualifie cette fusillade d'attentat terroriste ; la police enquete actuellement sur le contexte et les circonstances de cet attentat. Les autorites de Cracovie ont decrete un deuil jusqu'au 11 novembre. La presidence polonaise a annonce qu'un deuil national serait observe les 8 et 9 novembre.

items.title: Military hardware: Manufacturer seeks dedicated funding
items.description: The Chairman/CEO of EPAIL Nigeria, Kola Balogun, has called for dedicated government funding and stronger regulatory frameworks to accelerate Nigeria’s indigenous defence manufacturing industry. Balogun said sustainable development of the industry required deliberate government intervention, structured research funding and effective regulation of local manufacturers. He made the call in an interview with Newsman on the just-concluded Africa International Defence Exhibition (AFRIDEX) 2026. He said Nigeria needed a strong regulatory institution to establish standards, monitor research activities and ensure accountability in the utilisation of funds allocated to defence manufacturing. According to him, government funding should be directed towards clearly identified research priorities and solutions to the country’s peculiar security challenges. “We should not merely make budgetary provisions for defence manufacturing without clearly identifying the projects, research priorities and expected outcomes. “Government funding must be purposeful, dedicated and properly monitored.” Balogun argued that competition among indigenous manufacturers should be driven by government-funded research and innovation rather than unhealthy commercial rivalry. He said the government could identify specific security challenges and invite local manufacturers to develop competing technological solutions. “For instance, imagine a situation where we want to detect any object approaching our borders within a specified distance and automatically raise an alarm. “That should become a research challenge for indigenous defence manufacturers,” he said. He explained that manufacturers could receive initial funding to develop different solutions, after which the government would assess the proposals and support the most promising innovations. The EPAIL boss also advocated the establishment of defence industry incubation centres to provide platforms for researchers, engineers and manufacturers to develop and test innovative ideas. “Incubation centres are important because that is where research and innovation can take place. “They provide a clustered environment where individuals, researchers, engineers and companies can bring forward ideas, collaborate and conduct small-scale experiments,” he said. Balogun said the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON) and other relevant institutions should play leading roles in developing such innovation platforms. He stressed that effective regulation was equally necessary to control the production, distribution and sale of sensitive military equipment. According to him, manufacturers must know their end-users to prevent sensitive equipment from falling into the wrong hands. “There must be proper knowledge of the end-users to ensure that such equipment does not fall into the wrong hands,” he said. Balogun added that a properly regulated defence industry would create a pathway for indigenous manufacturers to grow, attract investment and contribute more meaningfully to national security. He said the successful development of Nigeria’s defence industry required sustained government commitment, strategic investment and an enabling environment for local innovation. items.title: What FIFA president said about Nigeria’s Flamingos after U-17 World Cup triumph
items.description: FIFA President Gianni Infantino has congratulated Nigeria’s Flamingos following their historic victory at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco. The Flamingos made history on Saturday night after defeating Japan’s Little Nadeshiko 2-1 in the final at Pitch 3 of the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat. Goals from Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku gave Nigeria a 2-0 lead before Fuki Ito scored a late consolation goal for Japan. Reacting to the victory, Infantino praised the Nigerian team for becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, describing their achievement as well deserved. “Congratulations to Nigeria, world champion U-17 Women’s World Cup of FIFA here in Rabat. First African team to ever win a (FIFA) Women’s U-17 World Cup — so many congratulations to Nigeria. Well deserved in the final,” he said. The FIFA president also congratulated Japan for finishing as runners-up and DPR Korea, who claimed third place in the tournament. He further commended Morocco for successfully hosting the competition, which brought together some of the world’s best emerging female football talents. Nigeria’s victory marks the country’s first title at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, having previously finished third at the 2022 edition in India. items.title: Ugandan woman in Nigeria for church crusade arrested with 87 cocaine wraps
items.description: …Intercepts UK, Australia-bound illicit drugs concealed in female head wears …Recovers multi-billion-naira Opioids, Loud in drug raids across states By: Kingsley Omonobi Operatives of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency have arrested a Ugandan woman who arrived the country for church crusade but turned out to be a courier when she was to return back with 87 wraps of Cocaine found hidden in her private part. According to the agency, “34-year-old Ugandan, Ms. Farida Nansubuga, came to Nigeria with members of her church for spiritual renewal at a prayer session in Lagos. But when it was time to go home, she chose a different path. “While the rest of her delegation flew back to Uganda, she stayed behind, not to pray some more, but to pick up a consignment of cocaine, which she hid in her private part in a bid to smuggle it into her country. “Her plan, however, came crashing down at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport (MMIA), Ikeja, Lagos, on Tuesday 3rd November 2026, when operatives of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) intercepted her at the screening point of Terminal 2 during a joint passenger screening exercise with aviation security personnel. “She was due to board a Ugandan airline flight to her home country. “A body search on her pointed to a substance concealed around her pelvic region, after which she was taken to a designated private search room for a secondary search. “This led to the recovery of eighty-seven (87) wraps of cocaine with a gross weight of 1.150 kilograms, strapped around her pelvic region and held in place beneath two layers of underwear. “During preliminary interview, the suspect, said she arrived in Nigeria on 29th October 2026 with members of her church for a prayer session at The Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN), Ikotun Egbe area of Lagos. “She claimed that after the prayer session, the other members of her delegation returned to Uganda while she stayed back to collect the illicit consignment on behalf of a friend, simply identified as Joy, who resides in Uganda. According to her, Joy directed her to a contact in Nigeria who arranged a vehicle to bring her to a hotel on the morning of her scheduled departure. “It was there, she said, that the man handed her the drug and instructed her to hide it beneath her clothing to beat security screening at the airport. “She claimed no definite fee was agreed for the trip, but that she expected to be paid not less than US$1,000 on successful delivery. In another interception at the Lagos airport, NDLEA operatives on Friday 6th November uncovered 750,000 tablets of Tapentadol 250mg, weighing 526 kilograms with a street value of N900 million, in a consignment from India declared as Paracetamol Tablets 500mg. The consignment, made up of eleven cartons packed in two wooden structures, arrived at the import shed of the airport on Tuesday 3rd November aboard an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Ahmedabad, India. Suspicious of the declaration, NDLEA officers placed the cargo under surveillance until a joint examination with officers of the Nigeria Customs Service and other sister agencies on Friday. The opioid pills were found in ten of the eleven cartons, while only the last carton contained paracetamol tablets as cover. Also at the import shed of the airport, NDLEA operatives on Wednesday 4th November intercepted 32 parcels of Loud, a strain of cannabis, weighing 16.15 kilograms, concealed inside two wooden sofas in a consolidated cargo that arrived from Houston, Texas, United States aboard a Turkish Airlines flight. A freight agent, Ibrahim Abdulwaheed Adewale, who came forward to clear the consignment was taken into custody. In a follow-up operation on Friday 6th November, a 34-year-old caterer from Ibadan, Oyo state, Adeoye Sarafa Ojo, walked in to collect the package was arrested. Adeoye claimed he was sent by a friend, Taiwo Anuoluwapo Olusegun. Similarly, NDLEA said a syndicate importing chemicals used in the production of Colorado, a synthetic cannabis, from the United Kingdom has come under the NDLEA hammer, following the interception of nine parcels of illicit substances hidden in two cartons of snacks tagged “Michael Tea Guy” in a consolidated cargo that arrived aboard an Air Peace flight from the UK on Friday 23rd October. Two of the parcels contained 1.20 kilograms of cannabis, while forensic analysis of the other seven parcels confirmed them to be chemicals used in making synthetic cannabis. A 51-year-old freight agent, Afolabi Abiodun Wale, who came to clear the consignment was arrested, while two more cartons for the same recipient later arrived from the UK aboard an Allied Air flight. A sting operation conducted between Monday 26th and Wednesday 28th October led to the arrest of Okwuite Benjamin Ojone, 51, when he took delivery of the four cartons. A search of the two additional cartons revealed three parcels concealed in two packs of detergent, weighing 3.30 kilograms, and eleven plastic bottles of mostly liquid substances weighing 16.25 kilograms, bringing the total seizure to 1.20kg of cannabis and 28.65kg of synthetic cannabis chemicals. At courier companies in Lagos, NDLEA operatives on Tuesday 3rd November intercepted 46 blocks of cannabis weighing 22.2 kilograms packed in two cartons going to the United Kingdom. Earlier, on Friday 30th October, they had intercepted 296 tablets of Swinol going to Australia from Lagos, as well as three shipments of tramadol going to the UK: 20 capsules from Benin City and 96 capsules from Sapele, Delta state, both concealed in vitamin C containers, and 600 tablets of Tramadol 225mg from Asaba hidden in female head wears. In Lagos, NDLEA operatives on Friday 6th November arrested a 32-year-old man, Abubakar Ali, at Marine Beach area of Apapa, where a stash of drugs was recovered from a small store he built inside the sitting room of his apartment. Items recovered include 1.06kg of Tramadol 250mg; 1.27kg of Tramadol 225mg; 400g of pregabalin capsules; 355g of diazepam; 200ml of codeine and 6.07kg of cannabis. In Ondo state, NDLEA operatives on Friday 6th November raided Odofin Road, Uso, where they recovered 148 bags of cannabis weighing 1,818 kilograms. Earlier same day, officers raided a cannabis farm in Board Forest, where they destroyed one hectare of cannabis plantation, recovered 242 kilograms of the drug and arrested a 36-year-old suspect, Itoro Linus Akpan. In neighbouring Ekiti state, a 53-year-old man, Agbo Paul Peter, was arrested at Osin Forest, Osin Ekiti, on Thursday 5th November with 216 kilograms of cannabis and cannabis seeds. In Edo state, NDLEA operatives on Friday 6th November intercepted a Golf saloon car loaded with nineteen bags of cannabis weighing 201 kilograms along Auchi–Ibillo road, Akoko Edo LGA, and arrested the driver, Abdulmumid Isah, 39, and a passenger, Danako Godwin, 25. In a related development, officers raided a notorious drug joint on Ihama Road, GRA, Benin City, where three suspects: Emmanuel Sunday, 25; Samuel Bala, 31; and Loveth Momodu, 20, were arrested with quantities of Colorado, Loud and cannabis. In Taraba state, operatives on stop-and-search duty at the NDLEA checkpoint in Lankaviri, Yorro LGA, arrested three suspects with a total of 283 blocks of compressed cannabis weighing 226.255 kilograms within two days. Also, on Thursday 5th November, Ibrahim Abdullahi, 45, was arrested with 156 blocks weighing 149.275kg, while Kabiru Usman, 25, was nabbed the same day with 80 blocks weighing 40.07kg. On Friday 6th November, Babangida Babayo, 32, was arrested with 47 blocks weighing 36.91kg. In Enugu state, a 57-year-old man, Celestine Uzochukwu Ejiakor, was arrested on Tuesday 3rd November at a checkpoint in Eke Obinagu with 44 blocks of cannabis weighing 22.5 kilograms. In another interception at the Ugwuoba checkpoint, officers arrested Godwin Shaapera, 40, with 24,000 capsules of Tramadol weighing 13.4 kilograms and 697 grams of ketamine. A suspect, Edugua Othuke, 30, was arrested by NDLEA operatives at Ozoro, Isoko North area of Delta state with 10.54kg skunk, 9.4kg cannabis seeds and 4.3grams of methamphetamine on Saturday 31st October 2026, while another suspect, Akpofure Tobore, 34, was nabbed with quantities of skunk, tramadol, rohypnol and laughing gas on Wednesday 4th November at Upper Agbarho, Ughelli area of the state. NDLEA said Commands and formations of the Agency across the country continued their War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) sensitization activities in schools, worship centres, work places and communities among others in the past week. These include: WADA enlightenment lecture to students and staff of St. Andrew Basic School, Oyo town, Oyo state; Government Technical College, Abakaliki, Ebonyi; Sa’ad College, Kano; and Inland Girls Secondary School, Onitsha, Anambra state, while the Zone 1 Command of NDLEA paid a WADA advocacy visit to the Emir of Bauchi, HRH Alhaji Rilwanu Sulaiman Adamu at his palace in Bauchi, among others. Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (Rtd), commended the officers, men and women of the MMIA, Lagos, Ondo, Ekiti, Edo, Delta, Taraba and Enugu Commands for the seizures and arrests. He noted that the case of the Ugandan woman is a sad reminder that drug cartels will stop at nothing, including exploiting faith and religious travel, to recruit couriers for their deadly trade. He urged officers across all commands to sustain the tempo of their supply and demand reduction efforts. items.title: Immigration Comptroller-General leads peace talks in Hamile after tragic border clash
items.description: The usually bustling border town of Hamile is on the verge of breathing a sigh of relief as the Comptroller-General of the Ghana Immigration Service (GIS), Samuel Basintale, led a high-stakes peace dialogue after a deadly explosion and subsequent clashes brought the town’s economy to its knees. The Comptroller-General’s intervention follows a tragic incident on November 3,on an unapproved route known as “Mountain Back 2”. The incident left one immigration officer dead, tricycle riders dead in a dynamite explosion, and 11 civilians injured during a confrontation with security forces. The visit, aimed at mending fractured relations between the community and security agencies, began with an inspection of the quarter guard parade at the forecourt of Ministries Block B. The Comptroller-General subsequently met with members of the Upper West Regional Security Council to obtain a comprehensive briefing on the volatile situation before travelling to Hamile. The Upper West Regional Police Commander, DCOP Francis Yiribaare, represented the council’s chairman. Providing an update on the situation, a security official said: “Just to add that the number of people who were injured in the course of those confrontations, nine so far have been discharged and scheduled for various dates for review. At the moment, the curfew is still ongoing, and we are enforcing it with all our might. We continue to keep our integrated team in Hamile to support the process, and we are also happy to witness the opening, the reopening, and the limited opening of the border. Business is not open today, but we are going to watch this opening.” The Comptroller-General, Samuel Basintale, warned that closing the border for even six hours could create severe traffic congestion, noting that large crowds gathering between stationary vehicles could become difficult to control. “Mali is now using it a lot for their cargo, and you close it for even six hours; look at the traffic that builds up there. I don’t think it is in the interest [of security], as that could even compound our security situation. Because if people mass up in between the vehicles, that becomes difficult to control. So it is better to process them quickly and let the trucks move than to lock it for whatever reason.” Upon arriving at the border post, the Comptroller-General was welcomed by the Hamile Centre Commander, Chief Superintendent Mohammed Abdul Mananu, who provided a detailed and harrowing account of the events of November 3. According to Commander Mananu, the crisis began when two officers attempted to stop a tricycle allegedly carrying dynamite along the Mountain Back 2 route. A massive explosion ensued, uprooting trees and leaving one officer dead and another fighting for his life. The chaos spilled over to the immigration office, where an angry mob of young people besieged the premises, hurling stones and burning tyres. When military and police reinforcements arrived, the situation escalated into gunfire, resulting in injuries to 11 residents. The Upper West Regional Police Commander, DCOP Francis Yiribaare, also briefed the delegation, assuring them that the security situation had since stabilised. He noted that the community had been cooperative and that the enforcement of a revised curfew, from 10:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m., had met no resistance. Speaking through the Assembly Member for the Happa Electoral Area, the Happa Divisional Chief, Hiller Dyaka Thomas Badukun III, welcomed the delegation and painted a grim picture of the town’s current state. He emphasised that the curfew had paralysed local businesses, preventing women from cooking and selling, while bringing cross-border trade to a standstill. Chairman of the Hamile Development Committee, Ibrahim Mohammed, adopted a conciliatory tone. He offered a heartfelt apology on behalf of the community, acknowledging its role in the unrest. He also passionately appealed for the immediate clearance of the massive backlog of cargo trucks stranded at the border, highlighting the severe hardships currently facing women and children. Adding to the community’s concerns, youth representative Mohammed Ibrahim assured the Comptroller-General that the youth were committed to ensuring that such violence never happened again. He appealed for the curfew to be lifted and requested that junior immigration officers exercise greater patience and restraint when interacting with residents and cross-border travellers. “We shouldn’t always come to war-war, but to jaw-jaw for peace to always prevail,” the Comptroller-General said, using the popular phrase to urge the community to prioritise dialogue over violence. He expressed deep concern over the use of unapproved bush routes by smugglers to traffic weapons and synthetic drugs such as Tramadol, which he warned were destroying the local youth. He challenged the community to stop shielding those involved in such illicit activities. Addressing the community’s grievances about unprofessional conduct by some officers, Mr Basintale acknowledged that prolonged postings could lead to complacency. He promised to transfer personnel who had overstayed their postings and committed to helping clear the backlog of trucks. Crucially, he announced a new “Community Engagement and Policing” initiative for the region. He also promised to recommend the lifting of the restrictive curfew to the Minister of the Interior by Monday, provided local leaders could guarantee sustained peace. The visit concluded with a sombre trip to the scene of the explosion at Mountain Back 2. There, the Comptroller-General and his entourage witnessed firsthand the sheer destructive force of the blast, a stark reminder of the fragile line between security operations and tragedy at the border.

items.title: Psychotropes en Algérie : des chiffres qui donnent froid dans le dos
items.description: Les chiffres des saisies de stupéfiants durant le premier semestre 2026 en Algérie font froid dans le dos. Il ne se passe pas un jour sans que la police, la gendarmerie et l’armée ne fassent état de la saisie de quantités considérables de stupéfiants, de psychotropes en particulier. Le dernier bilan semestriel dévoilé samedi par le directeur de l'Office national de lutte contre la drogue et la toxicomanie (ONLDT) est alarmant. Le directeur général de l’Office national de lutte contre la drogue et la toxicomanie (ONLDT), Tarek Kour, a rendu public, samedi 7 novembre à Alger, le bilan semestriel des saisies de drogues effectuées à travers le pays. « Le bilan du premier semestre 2026 porte des indicateurs inquiétants, notamment en ce qui concerne la prégabaline, dont les quantités saisies ont dépassé 36 millions de comprimés, dépassant ainsi le bilan global de l’année 2025 », a déclaré Tarek Kour, lors de son intervention au colloque sur les dimensions de la consommation de drogues, à la lumière des dispositions du Code de la route. Algérie : plus d’une tonne de cocaïne saisie durant le premier semestre 2026 Le bilan a fait état aussi de la saisie de plus d’une tonne de cocaïne et de 23 tonnes de cannabis, durant la même période. Pour sa part, le commandant de la Gendarmerie nationale, le général-major Ali Sidane, a relevé, au cours de ce colloque organisé au Cercle de l’armée de Beni Messous, que la dangerosité du fléau du narcotrafic réside dans « sa rapidité d'évolution et sa capacité à s'adapter aux mutations technologiques et socio-économiques ». Selon lui, les services de la gendarmerie ont démantelé 186 réseaux spécialisés dans le trafic de drogue et de substances psychotropes, durant les dix premiers mois de l’année 2026. Les opérations de la gendarmerie ont permis l’arrestation de 25 218 individus, dont 5264 ont été placés en détention. Au sujet de la sécurité routière, le commandant de la Gendarmerie a fait état de 161 accidents mortels et de 144 accidents corporels impliquant des conducteurs sous l’emprise de la drogue ou de substances psychotropes. La consommation de stupéfiants, notamment des substances psychotropes, s’est propagée ces dernières années en Algérie, touchant jusqu’aux écoliers. Pour y faire face, il a été procédé, en juillet 2025, au durcissement des peines prévues par la loi relative à la lutte contre le trafic de stupéfiants. Dans certains cas, les narcotrafiquants risquent la peine capitale avec exécution. Les premières condamnations à mort ont été prononcées par la Cour d’Alger, en octobre dernier. L’article Psychotropes en Algérie : des chiffres qui donnent froid dans le dos est apparu en premier sur TSA .
